fuller.text: This research paper asks whether a Transformer, a type of neural network built for language, can recognise what is in a picture with almost no changes. The authors cut each image into small square patches and feed them in the way words of a sentence would be fed in. They call the result the Vision Transformer, or ViT, and train it to label images.

fuller.text: In language, Transformers have become the standard tool, and they keep improving as models and datasets grow, with some passing 100 billion parameters. In vision, convolutional networks, or CNNs, still lead; they scan small windows across an image. Earlier attempts to bring attention into vision used special designs that were hard to run fast on modern chips. A plain Transformer could reuse the efficient tools already built for language.

fuller.text: Each patch, often 16 by 16 pixels, is flattened into a list of numbers and turned into a fixed-length vector by a learned linear step. A learned position code is added so the model knows where each patch came from. An extra learned "class token" is placed at the front, and its final state is used to decide the image's label.

fuller.text: The key idea is inductive bias: built-in assumptions about images, such as nearby pixels mattering together, which CNNs have and ViT mostly lacks. Trained on ImageNet, about 1.3 million images, ViT scores a few points below CNNs of similar size. With ImageNet-21k (14 million images) the gap closes, and with JFT-300M (303 million images) ViT pulls ahead. Tests on 9-million to 300-million-image subsets show ViT overfits small data more but wins from 90 million up.

fuller.text: After pre-training on lots of data, then fine-tuning, meaning extra training on a smaller target task, the main results are: The best model reaches 88.55% on ImageNet, 94.55% on CIFAR-100, and 77.63% across 19 VTAB tasks. It used 2.5k TPU core-days to pre-train, against 9.9k for the strongest CNN rival, BiT-L. In a controlled scaling study, ViT needed about 2 to 4 times less compute for the same accuracy, and showed no sign of levelling off.

fuller.text: Looking inside, the position codes learn the image's 2D layout by themselves, so nearby patches get similar codes. Some attention heads look across most of the image even in the first layers, while others stay local, rather like early CNN layers.

fuller.text: The authors note that training efficiency may also depend on choices like schedule and optimiser, not only the design. Self-supervised pre-training, learning by guessing hidden patches without labels, reached 79.9% on ImageNet, still 4% behind labelled pre-training. Applying ViT to tasks like finding and outlining objects remains to be done.

fuller.text: The conclusion is that a standard Transformer, treating an image as a sequence of patches, matches or beats top CNNs when pre-trained on large datasets. It does so while being relatively cheap to pre-train, and the authors expect further scaling to help.

brief.text: This paper tests whether a Transformer, a computer program built for language, can also recognize pictures. Transformers keep improving in language as they grow, but pictures are still mostly handled by an older design. The authors cut each image into small squares and feed them in like words in a sentence.

brief.text: Trained on a modest number of pictures, their Vision Transformer did slightly worse than the older design. Trained on 14 to 300 million pictures, it matched or beat the best programs. It also needed much less computer time to train. The main lesson: with enough training pictures, a simple general design can beat one built for images.
